issues.body:
### Description

Currently, SAML assertion decryption and key unwrapping operations are tightly coupled to local Java Cryptography Extension (JCE) providers. This limitation prevents deployments from offloading sensitive cryptographic operations to external Key Management Services (KMS) or Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) without invasive modifications to the core codebase.

As enterprise infrastructure shifts toward cloud-native security models, there is a growing requirement that private keys never reside directly in application memory. To support this, we need an abstraction layer that isolates the key unwrapping logic, allowing third-party extensions to intercept the decryption workflow and delegate the cryptographic handshake to external cloud providers (e.g., AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS).

### Value Proposition

* **Enhanced Enterprise Security:** Enables organizations with strict compliance mandates to keep their private keys isolated within dedicated hardware or cloud KMS solutions.
* **Extensibility without Core Bloat:** Avoids introducing cloud-specific vendor SDKs (AWS, Azure, etc.) into the core codebase, keeping dependencies lightweight while empowering the community to build custom extensions.
* **Seamless Upgrades:** Provides an entirely opt-in architecture, ensuring that existing users experience zero disruption or mandatory configuration updates.

### Goals

* **Pluggable Architecture:** Introduce an interface/SPI that exposes the necessary cryptographic parameters (algorithm URIs, encrypted bytes, and OAEP parameters) to custom provider implementations.
* **Contextual Awareness:** Ensure the decryption pipeline passes down the active application session/context so providers can securely resolve tenant-specific configuration settings.
* **Default Parity:** Maintain a default, out-of-the-box local JCE provider that seamlessly replicates all current capabilities, including key rotation, RSA-OAEP (with configurable digest/MGF), and RSA v1.5.
* **Graceful Fallbacks:** Automatically fall back to the legacy decryption execution path if no custom provider is registered or if the session context is entirely absent.

### Non-Goals

* **Out-of-the-Box Cloud Providers:** This issue does *not* include implementing specific cloud vendor integrations (such as an AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault provider) within this repository; those will live in separate, third-party extension modules.
* **Overhauling XML Parsing:** This change does not aim to replace or rewrite the underlying XML encryption utilities, but rather to intercept and abstract only the key unwrapping portion of the existing pipeline.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

**Implementation Status:** A companion Pull Request (https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/pull/49726) has already been opened to address this feature. We highly welcome feedback from maintainers and the community regarding the proposed architectural approach and interface design!
issues.title: saml: Introduce SPI for SAML assertion decryption and key unwrapping

issues.body:
### Description

Allow `UserStorageProvider` implementations to opt into storing service account users.

Currently `UserStorageManager.addUser` hardcodes all `service-account-*` users to local JPA storage, and `getServiceAccount` only consults local storage, regardless of what user federation providers are configured for the realm. This change introduces an optional capability interface, `UserServiceAccountProvider`, that a storage provider can implement to take ownership of service account creation and lookup. When such a provider is enabled, `UserStorageManager` routes service account users to it (in priority order) before falling back to local storage. Realms without a `UserServiceAccountProvider` are unaffected.

### Value Proposition

Deployments that use an external user store as the single source of truth (custom DB, IdM platform, etc.) currently end up with a split-brain: human users live in the external store while service account users are forced into Keycloak's local DB. This causes issues in several real-world setups:
- **Stateless / read-only Keycloak deployments** where the local DB is treated as disposable config and all identities must come from the external store. Today, enabling service accounts on a client silently writes a user row to the local DB.
- **Centralized governance / audit** where compliance requires all identities (both human and machine) to be inventoried, provisioned, and de-provisioned through one system.
- **Multi-cluster / multi-region deployments** that share a federated user store but run separate Keycloak databases; service account IDs and role mappings diverge between clusters.

This proposal is purely additive and opt-in meaning existing providers and realms see no behavioral change.

### Goals

- A capability interface (`UserServiceAccountProvider`) a `UserStorageProvider` can implement to handle `addServiceAccountUser` and `getServiceAccount`.
- `UserStorageManager` consults implementing providers in priority order, falling back to local storage when none handle the request.
- `AbstractUserAdapter` / `AbstractUserAdapterFederatedStorage` permit overriding `get`/`setServiceAccountClientLink` so adapters can persist the client link externally.
- Federated-storage cleanup (`preRemove`) runs for externally stored service accounts on client deletion.

### Non-Goals

- Changing the default behavior, we want service accounts to remain local unless a provider explicitly opts in.
- Making the built-in LDAP provider implement this interface.
- Promoting this to the public `server-spi` (it lives in `server-spi-private` until the contract is proven).
- Migrating existing locally stored service accounts to an external provider.

### Discussion

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/49738

### Notes

The implementation for this proposal is small and self-contained: one new interface in `server-spi-private`, a routing change in `UserStorageManager`, and relaxed Javadoc on the two abstract adapters. Any code change would include an integration test (`ServiceAccountUserStorageTest`) with a reference in-memory provider exercising create → `client_credentials` grant → client delete.
issues.title: Allow UserStorageProvider implementations to opt into storing service account users

issues.body:
### Description

## Summary
Keycloak has no built-in authenticator that adjusts the authentication 
flow based on a user's recent login failure history. The brute force 
subsystem tracks failures via UserLoginFailureModel, but there is no 
mechanism to use that data to dynamically escalate authentication 
within a flow.

## Problem
When a user account has experienced repeated login failures, there is 
no way for administrators to require stronger authentication for that 
specific user without applying that requirement globally to all users.

## Proposed Solution
Add a new Authenticator SPI implementation, RiskScoreAuthenticator, 
that reads the user's recent login failure count and escalates to an 
OTP challenge when failures reach a configurable threshold (default: 3). 
If failures are below the threshold, the authenticator passes through 
without interruption.

## Files Added
- RiskScoreAuthenticator.java (authenticator logic)
- RiskScoreAuthenticatorFactory.java (SPI factory registration)
- Updated META-INF/services/org.keycloak.authentication.AuthenticatorFactory
- RiskScoreAuthenticatorTest.java (integration tests)

### Value Proposition

Keycloak applies the same authentication flow to every login attempt
regardless of how many times that user has recently failed. This means
a suspicious login after repeated failures receives no additional
friction, while all legitimate users face the same static experience.

The RiskScoreAuthenticator closes this gap by reading a user's recent
login failure count and requiring OTP only when the count reaches a
configured threshold. Users with no failure history log in without
interruption. Accounts that have triggered repeated failures are
challenged with a second factor automatically, without any changes
to the global authentication policy.

### Goals

- Read the user's recent login failure count from UserLoginFailureModel
  during the authentication flow
- Escalate to an OTP challenge when the failure count reaches or
  exceeds the configured threshold (default: 3)
- Pass through without interruption when the failure count is below
  the threshold
- Register as a pluggable Authenticator SPI step that administrators
  can add to any authentication flow via the Admin UI
- Integrate with the existing AuthenticationProcessor chain without
  modifying it

### Non-Goals

- Does not replace or modify Keycloak's existing brute force protection
- Does not evaluate other risk signals such as IP address, device
  fingerprint, or login time
- Does not block login attempts outright; escalation is limited to
  requiring OTP
- Does not add new Admin Console screens beyond the existing flow
  editor
- Does not support per-client or per-user threshold configuration
  in this version

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: Add RiskScoreAuthenticator: escalate to OTP when login failure threshold is exceeded

issues.body:
### Description

The IETF mailmaint working group is currently developing two related Internet-Drafts that together define a modern, interoperable authentication and auto-configuration mechanism for email, calendar, and contact clients. The first is the OAuth Profile for Open Public Clients (draft-ietf-mailmaint-oauth-public), which specifies a tightly constrained OAuth 2.0 profile designed for native mail clients that have no pre-existing relationship with the authorization server. It mandates a specific combination of existing standards. The second draft, Automatic Configuration of Email, Calendar, and Contact Server Settings (draft-ietf-mailmaint-pacc), defines a complementary autoconfiguration mechanism by which mail providers publish a JSON document over HTTPS at a well-known URI, allowing clients to automatically discover server endpoints, supported protocols, and whether the provider supports the OAuth Public Clients profile.

The PACC draft is co-authored by Apple, which suggests that Apple Mail and related Apple platform clients are likely to adopt these drafts in the near future and will expect Identity Providers to conform to the OAuth Public Clients profile in order to support modern, password-free authentication against mail servers. When an organization uses Keycloak as its IdP in front of an IMAP, SMTP, JMAP, CalDAV, or CardDAV server, the mail client will follow the PACC autoconfiguration flow to discover the OAuth issuer and then proceed through the OAuth Public Clients profile against Keycloak. If Keycloak does not conform to what that profile mandates, the client will fail to authenticate.

It is possible that Keycloak already satisfies most or all of the requirements in the OAuth Public Clients draft. The primary purpose of this feature request is therefore not necessarily to trigger a large development effort, but rather to make the Keycloak maintainers aware of these drafts, since they will directly affect interoperability with a broad class of mail clients that use Keycloak as their IdP. 

Additionally, it would be very valuable if Keycloak maintainers could review the draft and send any technical comments or concerns to the IETF mailmaint mailing list (mailmaint@ietf.org). To my knowledge, the current drafts have not yet received review from IdP developers, and that perspective would be genuinely useful to the working group. If it is easier to share comments here in this issue, I am happy to relay them to the mailing list on your behalf.


### Value Proposition

Mail clients that implement PACC-based autoconfiguration and the OAuth Public Clients profile represent a growing share of the ecosystem, with Apple Mail as the most prominent near-term example. Organizations that deploy Keycloak as their IdP in front of mail infrastructure (IMAP, SMTP, JMAP, CalDAV, CardDAV) will face interoperability failures if Keycloak does not conform to the requirements of the OAuth Public Clients profile. The requirements that are most likely to need attention are: full support for Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) for unauthenticated native clients, strict conformance with the Authorization Server Metadata document (RFC 8414) including all mandatory fields the profile requires, support for the iss parameter in authorization responses (RFC 9207), support for Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), and token lifetime policies that satisfy the profile’s minimum requirements (access tokens valid for at least one hour, refresh tokens that do not expire prematurely). Ensuring and documenting Keycloak’s compliance with this profile will let administrators confidently use Keycloak as the IdP for mail infrastructure that serves modern clients, avoiding the need for workarounds, proxies, or custom client configuration.


### Goals

The goals of this feature request are to assess Keycloak’s current compliance with the requirements of draft-ietf-mailmaint-oauth-public (OAuth Profile for Open Public Clients) by reviewing the profile’s mandatory requirements against Keycloak’s existing behavior and configuration options. Where gaps exist, the goal is to implement the missing pieces or document the configuration needed to achieve compliance. Beyond implementation, a further goal is to provide documentation that explicitly addresses how to configure Keycloak to act as a compliant OAuth Public Clients profile authorization server for mail infrastructure scenarios.

### Non-Goals

This feature request is not asking Keycloak to implement a mail server, an IMAP or SMTP proxy, or any mail protocol handling. It is also not asking Keycloak to implement the PACC autoconfiguration mechanism itself, as that is the responsibility of the resource server or mail provider, not the IdP. This request does not cover custom or proprietary OAuth extensions beyond what the OAuth Public Clients profile mandates. It is also not a request to implement the informational IANA scope registry defined in the draft (e.g., urn:ietf:params:oauth:scope:mail), though documenting how administrators can configure equivalent scopes in Keycloak would be welcome. Finally, this request does not ask Keycloak to take any position on the drafts themselves; any technical feedback on the drafts should be directed to the IETF mailmaint working group and is separate from any implementation work in Keycloak.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: OAuth Profile for Open Public Clients

### Description

  Add post-quantum safe signature algorithms (ML-DSA) to Keycloak's WebAuthn/Passkeys implementation. Currently, all 8 supported WebAuthn signature algorithms are classical and vulnerable to quantum computers.
  ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is the NIST-standardized post-quantum replacement.

### Prerequisites
  - [ ] FIDO Alliance publishes PQC conformance test vectors
  - [x] webauthn4j merges ML-DSA support (webauthn4j/webauthn4j#1200)
  - [ ] At least one production browser/authenticator supports ML-DSA for WebAuthn

### Goals

  - Support ML-DSA COSE algorithm IDs (ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87) in WebAuthn policy, registration, and admin UI
  - Upgrade webauthn4j to a version with ML-DSA support
  - Should be wrapped-in the feature PQC_ML_DSA_WEBAUTHN delivered as preview unless specifications are finalised before release

### Non-Goals

  - Making ML-DSA the default algorithm — classical algorithms should remain the default
  - Deprecating or removing classical WebAuthn algorithms
  - Credential migration from classical to PQC algorithms — this will be handled separately when the ecosystem is ready


### Notes

  Blocked on upstream webauthn4j ML-DSA support (webauthn4j/webauthn4j#1200, PR webauthn4j/webauthn4j#1337). The maintainer is actively working on it — no Keycloak contribution needed at this stage, though Bouncy Castle as an alternative to JDK 24+ (JEP 497) for ML-DSA is worth raising upstream.

  No production PQC-capable FIDO2 authenticator or browser support exists yet — realistic timeline is 2027–2028. The standards layer is ready (WebAuthn L3 is algorithm-agnostic, ML-DSA COSE identifiers are registered at IANA).

  Investigation notes: 
- #48826

issues.body: ### Description Keycloak's SCIM Realm API (`--features=scim-api`) is missing three RFC 7644 capabilities that block enterprise provisioning flows (e.g. Microsoft Entra ID, Okta): Bulk Operations, valuePath bracket filters, and Sorting. **Three gaps identified:** 1. **Bulk Operations (RFC 7644 §3.7)** — `ServiceProviderConfig` reports `bulk.supported: false`. `POST /scim/v2/Bulk` with a valid `BulkRequest` does not return a `BulkResponse`. Single `POST /Users` works (201). https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7644/#section-3.7 2. **valuePath / bracket filters (RFC 7644 §3.4.2.2)** — Filters such as `emails[type eq "work"]` and `emails[primary eq true]` return 0 results even when users exist with matching email entries. Dot-notation filters (e.g. `emails.value co "example.com"`) work. https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7644/#section-3.4.2.2 3. **Sorting (RFC 7644 §3.4.2.3)** — `ServiceProviderConfig` reports `sort.supported: false`. `sortBy` / `sortOrder` are not supported. https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7644/#section-3.4.2.3 **Environment:** - Keycloak SCIM Realm API (experimental / technology preview) - Feature flag: `--features=scim-api` - Realm: `myrealm` (`scimApiEnabled=true`) - SCIM base URL: `http://localhost:8080/realms/myrealm/scim/v2` - Auth: OAuth2 client credentials (`scim-client` service account with `manage-users`, `view-realm`) ### Value Proposition Enterprise IdPs (Entra ID, Okta) rely on these RFC 7644 features: - POST /Bulk — batch user/group creates during initial sync instead of N separate requests - emails[type eq "work"] — filter users by email metadata (work/home/primary) - sortBy / sortOrder — predictable paging for large user sets Without these, adopters must build non-standard workarounds or avoid Keycloak as a full RFC-compliant SCIM target. ### Goals - POST /Bulk with BulkRequest/BulkResponse, bulkId resolution, failOnErrors - valuePath bracket filters on multi-valued attributes: emails[type eq "work"], emails[primary eq true], emails[type eq "work" and value co "@example.com"] - sortBy / sortOrder on GET /Users and GET /Groups - Advertise support accurately in ServiceProviderConfig - Clarify in docs which filter grammar is covered when filter.supported: true ### Non-Goals - Workaround implementations in third-party SCIM proxies - Breaking existing working behavior (userName eq, emails.value co, PATCH /Groups) ### Discussion _No response_ ### Notes Tested on Keycloak SCIM Realm API, --features=scim-api, realm: myrealm What works: POST /Users (201), simple filters (userName eq, emails.value co), PATCH /Groups, GET /ServiceProviderConfig What doesn't: - bulk.supported: false → POST /Bulk returns 401/500 - emails[type eq "work"] → 0 results (user exists with matching email) - sort.supported: false → sortBy/sortOrder ignored 1. Are bulk operations planned for a specific milestone (e.g. 26.7.0)? 2. Is valuePath bracket filter support planned for emails / phoneNumbers? 3. Should filter.supported: true be understood as full RFC 7644 grammar or dot-notation only? Related: #47590, #45287, #46213

### Description

The  26.6.3 introduced the following breaking change : 

> The wildcard comparison for valid redirect URIs does not affect the hostname anymore. Previously patterns like https://example.com* were accepted and lead to allow unintended domains like https://example.com.other.domain.com. Since this release, the hostname does not accept such type of wildcard and those patterns will be managed as if the wildcard is after the hostname https://example.com/*. The full wildcard for the hostname https://* is still accepted because its interpretation cannot be misunderstood.

In some case, one could need to allow multiple ports for a specific domain name, for instance in some pre-production environment. Would it be possible to support a syntax such as:

https://example.com:*/*


### Value Proposition

Reduces configuration overhead when multiple or dynamic ports are used for the same trusted domain, while preserving strict hostname validation and the security improvements introduced in 26.6.3.

### Goals

Allow a redirect URI pattern that:

- Matches a fixed scheme and hostname
- Allows any port via a wildcard (e.g. :*)
- Keeps existing path matching behavior unchanged

### Non-Goals

- No cross-domain matching (e.g. example.com.other-domain.com)

issues.body:
### Description

Switching Keycloak into an upgrade mode would make it effectively read-only except for a bare minimum functionality like login, logout and token refresh would be a building-block for allowing rolling minor release updates.

This should solve these problems: 
 
* When running a minor upgrade of Keycloak, this will usually include schema changes and database migrations. An old version running concurrently with the new version might update data so it is incompatible with the new version, and that data will never be migrated as the migration is already done.
* When an upgrade requires a rollback, changed data (like updated realm data or user data) will be lost.  

Update procedure with the new upgrade mode feature:
 
* Switch old version into upgrade mode by rolling all instances
* Deploy new version rolling, also in upgrade mode
* Verify the upgrade
* Redeploy new version rolling with upgrade mode disabled

In a first version, the mode would be toggled by a feature. Future versions might just flip a flag at runtime / via the API. 

### Value Proposition

* During the upgrade, users would still be able to log in and refresh their tokens, which is the most disruptive elements. This should deliver 90% of the value of rolling updates for minor releases. It is the same guarantee that we have for rolling patch releases. 
 
* It would allow to rollback to a database backup before the upgrade with minimal data loss (events stored in the database, lost logouts). Some gray area on revoked tokens and single-use tokens. 

### Goals

* Prevent all writes to the database with a Hibernate listener except for tables that are on the allow-list
   * All session and token tables would be allowed to write
   * Credentials, users and realm data would not be allowed for updates
* For any admin API request that is not GET or HEAD, return an error 
* Disable scheduled tasks where not essential during an upgrade (like Workflows, LDAP sync, cleanups) 
* Disable required actions, new user registration, broker first login flows for federation, possibly others to start simple
* A banner in the Admin UI telling that this instance is in upgrade mode
* Disable caches for users and offline/user sessions to as a safety measure in case there is a split brain.
* Persistent user sessions as a prerequisite 

Any future minor release would need to ensure that: 

* It can read from all tables after the new version has migrated the schema
* Session tables are read and written by both versions
* Maybe the previous minor release would need to minimal patch release to ensure the above
* No schema or data changes that lock the session tables or lock any other table that we read from for a longer period. An ALTER table would lock the table, but is fast when adding a column (usually).

### Non-Goals

* Switching the upgrade mode on/off at runtime (future)

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: Upgrade mode for Keycloak as a building-block for rolling minor release updates

issues.body:
### Description

When using Active Directory as an LDAP User Federation source, Keycloak currently fails to correctly interpret the lockoutTime attribute via standard mappers. In AD, lockoutTime is 0 when a user is not locked out, but becomes a largeBinary (Windows FILETIME timestamp) when a temporary lockout occurs due to bad password attempts.

Currently, when mapping this attribute to a Keycloak User Attribute, the largeBinary value is returned as an empty string, making it indistinguishable from the unlocked state (0). While Keycloak successfully detects disabled accounts via msad-user-account-control-mapper or UAC bitmask filters (e.g., (&(objectCategory=person)(sAMAccountName=*)(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))), these mechanisms cannot detect temporary lockouts. The UAC bitmask for lockout (512+16) is unreliable in modern AD environments and is often not set consistently, and import filters only control which users are synced — they do not provide real-time lockout state during authentication.

As a workaround, I attempted to map the raw userAccountControl integer into the user profile and handle the logic on the application side. However, this forces downstream applications to implement AD-specific bitmask parsing and lockout detection externally, which defeats the purpose of having an identity provider handle authentication state normalization. Keycloak should natively distinguish between a permanently disabled account and a temporarily locked out account at the LDAP federation layer, and surface this distinction during login with an appropriate error message.

### Value Proposition

**Accurate Authentication Feedback:** Enables Keycloak to return a specific "Account Temporarily Locked" error/message during login flows instead of a generic "Invalid credentials" or "Account Disabled" message, improving UX and reducing helpdesk tickets.

**Protocol Compliance:** Aligns Keycloak’s LDAP federation capabilities with actual Active Directory behavior, where lockout and disablement are distinct states.

**Reduced Client Complexity:** Eliminates the need for downstream applications to parse AD-specific userAccountControl bitmasks or handle binary LDAP attributes directly.

**Security Visibility:** Allows administrators to audit and monitor temporary lockouts separately from permanent account disablements within Keycloak events and admin console.

### Goals

- Correctly parse the AD lockoutTime binary/timestamp value through LDAP mappers without returning empty strings.
- Implement native detection of temporary AD lockouts within the LDAP storage provider or existing MSAD mappers.
- Expose the temporary lockout state as a first-class concept in Keycloak’s user model or authentication flow context.
- Provide appropriate error messages/responses during authentication when a user is temporarily locked out at the LDAP level.
- Maintain backward compatibility with existing msad-user-account-control-mapper and UAC-based filtering.

### Non-Goals

- Implementing write-back to reset AD lockout timers or unlock accounts via Keycloak (this should remain an AD administration task).
- Replicating AD’s lockout duration/threshold policy logic inside Keycloak; Keycloak should only read and reflect the current state.
- Supporting non-AD LDAP servers that do not use the Windows lockoutTime binary format (vendor-specific handling is acceptable here).
- Modifying the core User Model schema permanently if this can be achieved through mapper/storage provider enhancements.
- Handling password expiry or other UAC bits unrelated to the lockout vs. disabled distinction.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

## Design & Implementation Ideas:

1. Correct AD FILETIME Parsing for lockoutTime:
The immediate technical blocker is that the generic LDAP mapper treats lockoutTime as a UTF-8 string, which fails because AD returns it as a binary Octet String. The value is the exact timestamp when the account was locked out, stored in Windows FILETIME format (64-bit little-endian integer, 100-ns intervals since Jan 1, 1601 UTC).
A dedicated FILETIME converter in the LDAP storage provider must:
- Read 8 bytes in little-endian order.
- Convert to Unix epoch millis / ISO-8601 using the `11644473600s` offset.
- Handle 0 (not locked) and `0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` (locked indefinitely / admin unlock required).
Adding an Attribute Type like AD_FILETIME in mapper config would allow mapping lockoutTime directly into User Profiles as a readable timestamp.

2. Relying on AD Auto-Reset Behavior:
lockoutTime alone only tells when the lockout occurred. However, AD automatically resets lockoutTime to 0 once the domain’s lockoutDuration expires for automatic lockouts. Therefore, Keycloak does not need to read or calculate lockoutDuration separately. Simply parsing the current value of lockoutTime is sufficient:
- `0` → not currently locked.
- Valid non-zero timestamp → account is currently locked (automatic lockout still active).
- `0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF` → locked indefinitely (requires admin unlock). 

This eliminates the need for complex domain policy queries and significantly simplifies implementation.

3. Native Integration with msad-user-account-control-mapper:
The MSAD integration layer should natively interpret lockout state using the parsed lockoutTime with the logic above. During authentication, this should produce a distinct ACCOUNT_TEMPORARILY_LOCKED error, separate from ACCOUNT_DISABLED. All AD-specific timestamp logic stays encapsulated in the MSAD vendor module.
issues.title: Support AD lockoutTime attribute parsing to distinguish temporary lockouts from disabled accounts in LDAP Federation

### Description

The SSF transmitter is configured globally via SPI provider configuration (SsfTransmitterConfig), but operates per realm, this means metadata, streams, and event delivery are 
all realm-scoped. Allow selected transmitter settings to be overridden per realm via realm attributes (ssf.transmitter.*), resolved as: 
stream/client config -> realm attribute -> SPI config -> built-in default. 
Add a dedicated SSF tab in Realm Settings (gated on the ssf feature) hosting the transmitter enable toggle and the new settings.

### Value Proposition

Different realms represent different tenants with different receiver ecosystems. Realm-level overrides let each realm define its own 
transmitter policy (e.g. subject opt-in behavior, Apple SSE CAEP interop, subject format, signing algorithm) without affecting other 
realms or requiring server restarts, and make these settings manageable via the Admin API / IaC tooling.

### Goals

- Realm-overridable tenant-policy settings: defaultSubjects, subjectManagementEnabled, sseCaepEnabled, userSubjectFormat, signatureAlgorithm, criticalSubjectMembers
- Invalid realm values degrade gracefully (log + fall back to SPI value)
- SSF tab in Realm Settings with a Transmitter section, showing inherited server defaults for unset values

### Non-Goals

- Realm-level overrides for operational/security-posture settings such as push timeouts, metrics, allow-insecure-push-targets, verification timing stay SPI-only 
so realm admins cannot relax server-level constraints
- Changes to per-stream/per-client override behavior (existing precedence is preserved)
- Receiver-side realm configuration

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

Settings are plain realm attributes, so no new persistence or admin endpoint is required; the existing effective-config admin endpoint will reflect resolved realm values.

A dedicated SSF page later on also allows to specify common settings for SSF Receivers.

### Description

A Keycloak realm can contain multiple organizations representing B2B tenants and multiple clients representing applications. However, not every organization is necessarily entitled to access every client.

This feature proposes a client-level organization access policy with three modes:

- `Unrestricted`: Organization membership is not required.
- `Any organization`: The user must belong to an organization.
- `Specific organizations`: The selected organization must be authorized for the client.

Keycloak should enforce this policy before establishing a client session or issuing tokens, including when the user already has an SSO session.

### Value Proposition

This feature would provide centralized enforcement of application entitlements for B2B tenants. It would allow multiple organizations and applications to share one realm without duplicating access rules as user roles, implementing custom authenticators, or validating every organization-to-client relationship separately in each application.

### Goals

- Configure an organization access policy for each client.
- Support unrestricted access, access from any organization, and access from specific organizations.
- Support a many-to-many relationship between organizations and clients.
- Verify both user membership and the selected organization's entitlement.
- Enforce the policy during authentication, SSO reuse, and applicable token refresh operations.
- Manage the configuration through the Admin Console and Admin REST API.
- Preserve the current unrestricted behavior for existing clients.

### Non-Goals

- Allowing organizations to create, own, or administer clients.
- Restricting which identity provider an organization or client must use.
- Replacing roles, scopes, groups, or Authorization Services.
- Immediately revoking already-issued access tokens when an entitlement is removed.
- Defining organization-aware access for service accounts or machine-to-machine flows.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: Organizations: Enforce organization membership and entitlements per client

### Description

Currently, Keycloak's Authentication SPI and FormAction SPI are tightly coupled to browser-based HTTP redirects and FreeMarker (.ftl) template rendering.

When building a modern Single Page Application (like React, Next.js, or Angular) that requires a fully custom, native frontend UI, developers encounter blocking errors (opaque redirects, CORS failures, and session state drops) when attempting to consume multi-step authentication flows—such as custom Mobile OTP registration headlessly.

### Value Proposition

Value Proposition
As the industry increasingly moves toward headless architectures and modern Single Page Applications (React, Next.js, Angular), developers need full control over their authentication UI without resorting to browser redirects or iframe workarounds.

Currently, Keycloak's Authentication Flow engine is tightly coupled to browser-based redirects and FreeMarker (.ftl) rendering. When SPAs attempt to consume multi-step flows (e.g., custom Mobile OTP registration) headlessly, they encounter CORS failures, opaque redirects, and dropped session states. To bypass this, developers are forced to write custom RealmResourceProvider REST endpoints—essentially rebuilding Keycloak's flow logic, state management, and brute-force protections from scratch.

Introducing native headless support for the flow engine will drastically reduce development overhead, prevent security fragmentation, and make Keycloak a first-class citizen for modern SPA architectures.

### Goals

1. Provide a standardized, API-driven mechanism to execute Keycloak Authentication Flows headlessly.
2. Enable SPAs to trigger a flow, receive a JSON representation of the current step/required fields, and submit 
3. JSON payloads to progress to the next step.
4. Ensure all existing built-in flow protections (rate limiting, brute-force protection, authentication session state) work seamlessly over API without requiring browser cookies or HTTP 302 redirects.
5. Allow developers to leverage the visual Keycloak Flow builder in the admin console for SPA-driven authentication.

### Non-Goals

1. Deprecating or replacing the existing FreeMarker (.ftl) rendering engine. Traditional server-rendered flows will remain fully supported.
2. Building or maintaining specific frontend SDKs (React, Vue, etc.) within the core Keycloak repository. The focus is strictly on standardizing the JSON API contract.
3. Modifying the underlying OAuth2/OIDC specification. This proposal only addresses the internal step-by-step UI flow execution prior to token issuance.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

1. Content Negotiation: Modify the Authenticator and FormAction SPIs to respect the Accept header. If a client requests Accept: application/json, Keycloak should bypass .ftl rendering.
2.  JSON State Representation: Instead of returning an HTML page, Keycloak returns a standardized JSON object detailing the current flow state. For example:```
json
{
  "flowId": "mobile-otp-registration",
  "executionId": "1234-abcd",
  "step": "otp_verification",
  "requiredFields": ["otp_code"],
  "messages": [{"type": "info", "text": "An OTP has been sent to your mobile."}]
}
```

1. Stateless/Tokenized Execution: To solve the issue of SPAs struggling with traditional session cookies during cross-origin requests, Keycloak could issue a temporary, short-lived "flow continuation token" (JWT) in the initial response. The SPA would pass this token in the Authorization header of subsequent requests to maintain the AuthenticationSessionModel state across steps.
2. Integration with Existing SPIs: The Authenticator SPI interface could be expanded with a default method Response challengeApi(AuthenticationFlowContext context) which developers can override to define exactly what JSON payload is returned when their custom step is reached in headless mode.
issues.title: Feature Request: Native Headless (API-only) Support for multi-step Authentication Flows (React/SPA)

issues.body:
### Description

Introduce **native stateful API key management in Keycloak** as a first-class credential and authentication mechanism.

Keycloak currently provides stateless authentication through OAuth2/OIDC access tokens, typically represented as JWTs. However, there is no native mechanism for creating and managing **stateful API keys** that are associated with an existing Keycloak user or service account and can have their own permissions, expiration, rotation, and revocation lifecycle.

The proposed feature is to introduce API keys directly into Keycloak's existing identity and authorization model.

An API key would belong to a Keycloak identity and would be independently manageable:

```text
User / Service Account
        |
        +-- API Key A
        |      ├── Permission: agents:read
        |      ├── Permission: agents:execute
        |      ├── Expires: 90 days
        |      └── Status: Active
        |
        +-- API Key B
               ├── Permission: agents:read
               ├── Permission: models:read
               ├── Expires: 1 year
               └── Status: Active
```

### Proposed API Flow

The feature should expose APIs for the complete API-key lifecycle:

#### 1. Create an API Key

```http
POST /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{user-id}/api-keys
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
```

```json
{
  "name": "production-agent",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-19T00:00:00Z",
  "permissions": [
    "agents:read",
    "agents:execute"
  ]
}
```

The response should return the generated API key **only at creation time**, together with its metadata.

```json
{
  "id": "key-123",
  "name": "production-agent",
  "apiKey": "<generated-secret>",
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-19T00:00:00Z",
  "status": "ACTIVE"
}
```

The secret should not be retrievable again after creation.

#### 2. List API Keys

```http
GET /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{user-id}/api-keys
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
```

The response should contain key metadata but never the actual secret:

```json
[
  {
    "id": "key-123",
    "name": "production-agent",
    "status": "ACTIVE",
    "expiresAt": "2026-11-19T00:00:00Z",
    "lastUsedAt": "2026-08-19T10:30:00Z"
  }
]
```

#### 3. Revoke an API Key

```http
DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{user-id}/api-keys/{key-id}
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
```

Revocation should take effect immediately.

#### 4. Rotate an API Key

```http
POST /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{user-id}/api-keys/{key-id}/rotate
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>
```

A new secret should be generated while retaining the API key's identity, metadata, and configured permissions.

#### 5. Validate an API Key

An API or API gateway should be able to validate a presented API key against Keycloak:

```http
POST /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/api-key/introspect
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

api_key=<api-key>
```

The validation response should provide the associated identity and authorization context:

```json
{
  "active": true,
  "user_id": "user-123",
  "client_id": "client-123",
  "key_id": "key-123",
  "permissions": [
    "agents:read",
    "agents:execute"
  ],
  "expiresAt": "2026-11-19T00:00:00Z"
}
```

For an expired, disabled, or revoked key:

```json
{
  "active": false
}
```

#### Authorization

The API key should integrate with Keycloak's existing authorization capabilities rather than introducing an independent authorization model.

The important distinction is that **permissions should be associated with the individual API key**, not only with the user.

For example:

```text
User: john.doe

API Key: production
    agents:read
    agents:execute

API Key: monitoring
    agents:read
    models:read
```

Both keys belong to the same Keycloak identity, but compromising the `monitoring` key should not provide the permissions assigned to the `production` key.

The API-key authentication flow should therefore be:

```text
Client
   |
   | X-API-Key: <secret>
   v
API / API Gateway
   |
   | Validate API Key
   v
Keycloak
   |
   +--> Locate API Key
   +--> Check Active/Revoked status
   +--> Check Expiration
   +--> Resolve Keycloak Identity
   +--> Resolve Key Permissions
   |
   v
Authentication + Authorization Context
   |
   v
API
```

This would allow Keycloak to provide the equivalent of a centralized:

**API Key → Identity → Permissions**

relationship.

The API-key mechanism should complement, rather than replace, the existing OAuth2/OIDC JWT authentication mechanisms.

The primary value is to provide a **stateful, individually revocable, permission-scoped credential** while reusing Keycloak's existing users, service accounts, authorization policies, permissions, and Fine-Grained Authorization capabilities.


### Value Proposition

Native API key support would extend Keycloak's identity and access-management capabilities to use cases where OAuth2/OIDC JWTs are not the most appropriate credential mechanism.

The feature would provide:

* **Centralized credential management** — API keys can be created, managed, revoked, and audited directly within Keycloak.
* **Fine-grained access control** — Individual API keys can have their own scopes and permissions.
* **Immediate revocation** — Unlike stateless JWTs, a stateful API key can be invalidated immediately.
* **Credential lifecycle management** — Support for expiration, rotation, disabling, and regeneration.
* **Reuse of existing identities** — API keys can be associated with existing Keycloak users or service accounts.
* **Reduced infrastructure complexity** — Applications and API gateways would not need to maintain a separate API-key database and identity mapping.
* **Consistent authorization** — Existing Keycloak roles, groups, scopes, policies, resources, and permissions can potentially be reused.
* **Improved security and governance** — API-key creation, usage, expiration, and revocation can be centrally managed and audited.

This would complement Keycloak's existing OAuth2/OIDC capabilities rather than replace them, giving organizations a choice between stateless tokens and stateful API credentials depending on their use case.


### Goals

The feature should provide the following capabilities:

### API Key Lifecycle

* Create API keys for Keycloak users and service accounts.
* Support multiple API keys per identity.
* Give each API key a human-readable name/description.
* Support enabling and disabling API keys.
* Support immediate revocation.
* Support API key rotation.
* Support configurable expiration dates.
* Track creation and modification timestamps.
* Track last-used information where feasible.

### Authentication

* Allow APIs and API gateways to authenticate requests using an API key.
* Resolve the API key to its associated Keycloak identity.
* Provide a mechanism for consuming services/gateways to validate an API key.
* Return the associated identity and authorization context after successful validation.

### Authorization

* Allow permissions/scopes to be associated with individual API keys.
* Integrate API keys with Keycloak's existing authorization model.
* Reuse existing roles, groups, scopes, policies, resources, and permissions where appropriate.
* Support different API keys belonging to the same user having different access levels.

For example:

```text
User: john.doe

API Key: production
    agents:read
    agents:execute

API Key: monitoring
    agents:read
    models:read
```

### Administration

* Provide API-key management through the Keycloak Admin Console.
* Provide appropriate Admin REST APIs for API-key lifecycle management.
* Provide user-facing API-key management where appropriate.
* Expose relevant audit events.
* Ensure API-key secrets are securely stored and are not retrievable after creation.

### Security

* Use cryptographically secure, sufficiently long API-key values.
* Store secrets securely, preferably in a non-reversible form where possible.
* Display the secret only during initial creation.
* Support secure rotation.
* Prevent API keys from being exposed through logs or administrative APIs.


### Non-Goals

The following capabilities are considered out of scope for the initial implementation:

* **Replacing OAuth2/OIDC** — API keys should complement existing OAuth2/OIDC authentication rather than replace JWT-based authentication.
* **Replacing Keycloak Authorization Services** — The feature should leverage existing authorization capabilities rather than introduce an entirely separate authorization framework.
* **API gateway functionality** — Keycloak should manage the identity and API-key credential; rate limiting, request routing, load balancing, and API gateway functionality should remain the responsibility of the appropriate gateway layer.
* **Application-specific authorization logic** — Individual applications should continue to define application-specific authorization requirements where necessary.
* **Secrets/password manager functionality** — API keys should not become a general-purpose secret-management solution.
* **Unlimited credential customization** — The initial implementation does not need to support arbitrary custom metadata or complex credential policies beyond the core API-key lifecycle and authorization requirements.
* **Replacing service accounts** — API keys should work with existing Keycloak users and service-account concepts rather than introducing another identity type unnecessarily.
* **Mandatory support for every API-key transport format** — Supporting common mechanisms such as `Authorization: Api-Key` or `X-API-Key` is sufficient initially; additional formats can be considered separately.


### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: Feature Request: Native Stateful API Key Management with Fine-Grained Permissions

### Description

### [Feature]: Security notifications for logins from untrusted devices or IP addresses

### Is your feature request related to a problem?
Yes. Currently, if an unauthorized user (e.g., an attacker who compromised credentials) logs into a user's account, the legitimate account owner remains unaware of the breach unless they manually check their active sessions in the personal dashboard. This leaves accounts vulnerable to undetected malicious activity.

### Solution
We need to implement automated security alerts for new and untrusted login attempts. Specifically:
1. **Trigger:** Detect when a user authenticates from an untrusted device (a device not previously used) or an untrusted IP address (an IP location not seen before for this account).
2. **Action:** Automatically send a security notification to the user (via Email/Push/SMS depending on system configuration).
3. **Notification Content:**
   - Details of the login event (time, approximate location, device type/browser).
   - A direct link to their personal dashboard/account settings.
   - Clear guidelines on how to immediately reset their password and terminate all active sessions if they do not recognize the activity.

### Describe alternatives you've considered
An alternative would be requiring Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) or email verification *before* allowing the login from a new device. While MFA is a stronger security measure, implementing post-login security notifications is a critical baseline feature that provides immediate visibility without adding friction to the user experience.

### Value Proposition

### Additional context
This feature significantly improves account security and helps users quickly mitigate security breaches before extensive damage is done.

### Goals

1. **Trigger:** Detect when a user authenticates from an untrusted device (a device not previously used) or an untrusted IP address (an IP location not seen before for this account).
2. **Action:** Automatically send a security notification to the user (via Email/Push/SMS depending on system configuration).

### Description

Currently, Keycloak allows configuring User Federation (like LDAP) sync periods using interval-based timers (Full Sync Period and Changed Users Sync Period in seconds). However, there is no way to anchor these syncs to a specific time of day.

We need the ability to schedule synchronization at specific hours (e.g., "Daily at 00:00, 04:00, 07:00") or using standard CRON expressions, while keeping the ability to trigger manual synchronization via the admin UI button.

### Value Proposition

Interval-based timers calculate the next execution relative to the server start time or the last successful sync. Over time, this causes synchronization tasks to shift and unpredictably land on peak operational hours. This behavior causes high database and CPU loads, degrading overall system performance for end-users.

Optimizing the sync schedule to run strictly during off-peak hours (e.g., at night) is crucial for production environments with large user bases.

### Goals

1. CRON/Scheduled expression support: Add an option in the User Federation settings to switch from interval-based syncing (seconds) to a specific time schedule or a CRON expression (e.g., 0 0 0,4,7,11,15,20 * * ?).

2. Preserve Manual Sync: Ensure that introducing scheduled syncs does not affect or disable the "Synchronize all users" and "Synchronize changed users" buttons in the Admin Console. Manual sync must remain available at any time.

### Description

Add an **User Attribute Template Importer** OIDC Identity Providers that allows concatenating multiple IdP claims and static strings into a single target Keycloak user attribute using template expressions.

Currently, Keycloak provides the `Username Template Importer`, which supports template-based claim combination (e.g. `${CLAIM.email}_${CLAIM.phone_number}`) specifically for `username`. However, the standard `Attribute Importer` only supports 1:1 mapping from a single incoming claim to a user attribute.


### Value Proposition

In many identity federation architectures, upstream Identity Providers (IdPs) provide identity data across separate claims that client applications need combined into a unified format.

A client application requires a complete, formatted user attribute such as a normalized phone number (e.g. `+8612322334455`), but the upstream Identity Provider provides two separate token claims:
- `"region_code": "+86"`
- `"phone_number": "12322334455"`

An additional use case is attribute based access control, so that multiple upstream claims can be combined into one attribute and a Keycloak client application can check for presence of the claim without client side authorization logic needed.
Example: 
- `"country": "US"`
- `"sales_org": "03"`

When this concatenated to a claim `"sales_region":"US_03"` a client application does not need to evaluate multiple claims.

Without template support for general user attributes, administrators must either:
1. Force downstream applications to ingest multiple separate claims and perform concatenation themselves.
2. Implement and maintain a custom `IdentityProviderMapper` Java SPI plugin on every Keycloak deployment.

Providing a native template mapper for user attributes aligns feature parity with the existing `Username Template Importer`.

### Goals

Introduce a new Identity Provider Mapper: `Attribute Template Importer` with the same claim and string concatenation possibility as the "Username Template Importer".

**Additional: Multi-value support**
Support the case that exactly one of the claims in the template is an array, resulting in an array of concatenated values with same length as the source array.
If more than one template claims provide arrays, the mapper can set an empty value and log a warning.


### Non-Goals

-

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

### Description

Currently, we have clients in Keycloak that use a custom protocol (`custom://...`) to redirect users back to a native app. This works perfectly fine, but has the unfortunate side-effect that the browser tab remains "stuck" at the previous page (blank, or the page from our upstream IdP) - this is because Keycloak performs an HTTP redirect.

The feature we propose would (optionally) change Keycloak post-login behaviour: instead of an HTTP redirect, Keycloak should render a normal web page as "post-login landing page". This page can then show a user message like "It is now safe to close this window", while performing a JavaScript redirect (`window.location.href`) to the original redirect URI.

### Value Proposition

Having the custom "landing page" enhances clarity to user, by explicitly showing that sign-in is complete and that the tab or window can now be closed. This is useful both immediately upon signin, but also later when the user might "stumble" across an old tab that was used for logging in.

- Provide a landing page for users after logging in and before being redirected to the (native) client. This changes the redirect from an HTTP redirect to a JS redirect.
- Provide a client setting to enable this landing page
- Optionally automatically enable this setting for non-web (http/https) URI schemes.

issues.body: ### Description Hello Team, I would like to raise a ticket regarding password complexity enforcement in Keycloak. Issue: The application currently allows users to create passwords with characters repeated more than four times(e.g. '111133345') consecutively and also permits common keyboard patterns (e.g., 'qwerty', '12345'). This weakens password strength and increases the risk of compromise. Restrict consecutive character repetition beyond four. Block common keyboard sequences. Ensure compliance with minimum length, mixed character types, and dictionary word restrictions. ### Value Proposition The value of enforcing stronger password complexity in Keycloak is significant for both security and compliance. Here’s how it helps: Enhanced security → Prevents weak passwords like repeated characters (“AAAAA”) or predictable keyboard patterns (“qwerty”), which are easy for attackers to guess or brute-force. Reduced risk of compromise → Stronger rules make credential stuffing and dictionary attacks far less effective, protecting user accounts and sensitive data. Compliance alignment → Meets Accenture’s Identification and Authentication Standard, ensuring the application adheres to corporate and industry security policies. User accountability → Encourages users to create unique, complex passwords, fostering better security hygiene across the organization. Operational resilience → Reduces the likelihood of breaches that could disrupt services, damage reputation, or incur regulatory penalties. ### Goals For a password complexity feature in Keycloak, the capabilities should be clearly defined so both the vendor and stakeholders understand what it enforces. Here’s a structured view: Character repetition control → Prevent users from repeating the same character more than four times consecutively. Keyboard pattern detection → Block predictable sequences like “qwerty,” “asdf,” or “12345.” Mixed character enforcement → Require inclusion of uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and special characters. Minimum length requirement → Enforce a baseline length (e.g., 12 characters) to strengthen entropy. Dictionary word restriction → Disallow common words or known weak passwords from being used. Configurable policy settings → Allow administrators to adjust rules to meet evolving compliance standards. Audit and reporting → Provide logs or reports showing password policy enforcement for compliance checks. ### Non-Goals Biometric authentication → The feature will not introduce fingerprint, facial recognition, or other biometric login methods. Multi-factor authentication → MFA setup and enforcement are separate security controls, not part of password complexity rules. ### Discussion _No response_ ### Notes _No response_

### Description

It has been observed that sensitive information, such as process IDs, was revealed as part of the URL. This practice poses a security risk, as passing sensitive information in URLs can lead to potential exploitation by attackers.

Impact:

Sensitive data in URLs may be logged in browser history, server logs, and third-party monitoring tools.

Attackers could leverage exposed process IDs or session variables to launch further attacks, including session hijacking or information leakage.

Remediation:

Never pass sensitive information as part of the URL.

Use secure session management practices, such as storing session identifiers in cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags.

Ensure sensitive data is transmitted via POST requests or stored securely in server-side sessions.



### Value Proposition

The feature delivers tangible business and technical benefits by addressing critical pain points and enabling measurable outcomes.

Enhanced security → Prevents exposure of sensitive information, reducing risk of data leakage and compliance violations.

Operational efficiency → Streamlines processes by eliminating insecure practices, lowering incident response overhead.

Trust and compliance → Strengthens stakeholder confidence by aligning with industry standards and regulatory requirements.

Scalability and maintainability → Provides a secure foundation that supports future growth without introducing vulnerabilities.

User confidence → Ensures end‑users interact with the system safely, improving adoption and satisfaction.

### Goals

The feature is designed to deliver secure, reliable, and user‑friendly functionality. Specifically, it should provide:

Secure data handling → Ensure sensitive information (session variables, process IDs, tokens) is never exposed in URLs.

Robust session management → Store session identifiers in secure cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags, preventing unauthorized access.

Safe request transmission → Use POST requests or server‑side storage for sensitive data, avoiding query string exposure.

Compliance alignment → Meet industry security standards and regulatory requirements by eliminating insecure practices.

Operational resilience → Reduce risk of exploitation, replay attacks, and information leakage through hardened design.

### Non-Goals

To avoid scope creep and misaligned expectations, the feature will not provide the following capabilities:

Biometric authentication → Fingerprint, facial recognition, or other biometric login methods are outside the scope.

Multi‑factor authentication → MFA setup and enforcement are separate security controls, not part of this feature.

Password expiration policies → Rotation schedules and expiration rules are managed independently.

Single sign‑on integration → SSO capabilities are not impacted by this feature.

User education or training → Awareness campaigns or training materials are not included.

Account recovery mechanisms → Password reset flows, recovery questions, or backup codes remain out of scope.

issues.body:
### Description

Provide a built-in and efficient way to retrieve the timestamp of the last successful user authentication through the Admin API.

The timestamp should be stored and maintained by Keycloak and exposed as part of the user administration model, without requiring administrators to query and aggregate historical login events.

### Value Proposition

**Problem Statement**

Today, obtaining the last successful login time of a user is not straightforward.

The information can only be derived from stored LOGIN events, which requires:

Enabling event persistence.
Retaining historical events for a sufficiently long period.
Querying and filtering events for each user.
Computing the most recent LOGIN event.

This approach turns an operational user attribute into an audit-log query problem.

For large installations with millions of events, querying login history can become expensive and difficult to use for routine administrative tasks.

### Goals


**Dormant Account Management**

Administrators often need to:

Identify users who have not authenticated for N days.
Disable inactive accounts.
Delete dormant accounts according to security policies.

A dedicated last authentication timestamp would make these operations significantly easier.

**Security and Compliance**

Organizations frequently need to know:

When a user last authenticated.
Whether an account appears abandoned.
Whether a privileged account has been inactive for an unusual period.
IAM Integrations

External IAM, governance, and reporting tools often consume user metadata through the Admin API.

Having direct access to a last authentication timestamp would eliminate the need for event log analysis and custom extensions.

**User Administration**

Administrators commonly expect to see information such as:
Last login: 2026-08-15T12:34:56Z
directly when managing users.

Maintain a built-in timestamp representing the most recent successful authentication of a user.

Characteristics:

Stored in UTC.
Updated after successful authentication.
Available through Admin REST APIs.
Available through the Java Admin Client.
Queryable and filterable for administration purposes.

Example:
`{
    "id": "12345678",
    "username": "jdoe",
    "lastSuccessfulAuthentication": "2026-08-15T12:34:56Z"
}`

### Non-Goals

This proposal does not aim to:

* Store a complete authentication history on the user object.
* Replace the existing Events subsystem or audit capabilities.
* Provide detailed activity analytics or reporting.
* Track token refreshes, session refreshes, or user activity beyond successful authentication events.
* Introduce new user-configurable attributes managed by administrators.
* Define automatic user cleanup, suspension, or deletion policies.
* Change existing event retention mechanisms.
* Persist client, group, or realm activity metrics.
 
This proposal is limited to exposing a single, efficiently maintained timestamp representing the last successful authentication of a user.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

**Design Discussion**

The primary goal of this proposal is to expose a user's last successful authentication timestamp through supported administration APIs.

The implementation mechanism is intentionally left open.
Possible approaches could include:
- Maintaining a dedicated activity tracking store.
- Persisting the timestamp alongside user-related metadata.
- Introducing a generic usage-tracking framework that could also support other entities such as clients, groups, or service accounts.
 
The important aspect is not where the information is stored, but that it can be retrieved efficiently without requiring administrators to query and aggregate historical LOGIN events.

The solution should also:

- Avoid dependency on event retention policies.
- Scale to large deployments with millions of users and events.
- Remain compatible with clustered deployments.
- Store timestamps in UTC.
- Be accessible through Admin APIs and Java Admin Client representations.

This proposal does not require full login history persistence and only focuses on the most recent successful authentication timestamp.
issues.title: Expose User Last Successful Authentication Timestamp

issues.body:
### Description

We use Keycloak Organizations for tenancy. Each customer organization has members and organization groups in Keycloak, and on our side owns projects.

We wanted to express "this organization group can do X on this project". Authorization Services looked like the right tool, but it is scoped to a client: resources, policies and permissions all live under `/admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{client-uuid}/authz/resource-server/`, and there is no organization dimension. Organization groups also cannot be used in group policies, which take realm group IDs.

That leaves registering every customer's projects as resources under one shared client, or doing authorization outside Keycloak. We did the latter.

The shared-client option didn't work for us because:

- it is one flat resource namespace across all organizations, and since names are unique per owner and the Protection API returns 409 on collision, we would encode organization and project IDs into resource names
- a resource is owned by the client or by a user, so there is no way to say it belongs to an organization
- our realm config is version controlled and imported at startup, so customer data would end up inside it
- organization groups still cannot appear in policies, so the grant we wanted stays inexpressible without a custom policy provider

Organization groups (26.6) and role mapping onto them (26.7) gave organizations an isolated identity model. Authorization did not follow.

### Value Proposition

Any B2B SaaS using Organizations for tenancy has per-tenant objects and the same question about them. Today Organizations covers identity but not authorization, so adopters build that half elsewhere and the policy engine goes unused.

### Goals

- resources and permissions that belong to an organization, isolated the way organization groups are
- organization groups usable in policies
- managed under the organization in the Admin REST API

A smaller version that would still help: allow organization groups to be referenced by group policies, even if resources stay realm-level.

### Non-Goals

- delegating client management to organizations, meaning client CRUD, secrets and redirect URIs. That is #42781, and this does not need it
- organization roles, covered by #40585. A role says what a member is within an organization; this is about what they can act on
- changing realm-level Authorization Services for existing users
- a new policy language or evaluation engine

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

#42781 would give us this through organization-owned clients, since a resource server is a client, though it argues for self-service client registration rather than the authorization case. "Manage Clients and Service Accounts" is also unchecked on the Organizations epic #30180.
issues.title: Organization-scoped resources in Authorization Services

issues.body:
### Description

Keycloak has experimental feature `OID4VC_VCI_REST_CREDENTIAL_OFFER` . This task is about review of that feature and figure whether to support it or remove it.

#### Details

Keycloak has custom (not specs compliant) REST endpoint to create credential offer for specific user. Endpoint returns QR code (or deep link) in the response. Then administrator is responsible for sharing the QR code (or deep link) somehow with the user (this happens outside of Keycloak), so user can redeem his credential by himself. As of now, the endpoint is possible to be invoked only by "administrator" with the realm role `credential-offer-create` .

The endpoint can be also triggered by user himself for the case when he creates credential-offer for himself. As of now, any user can create credential-offer for himself without any restrictions and user does not need to be in any role.

#### Possible issues with current approach

**Security:** Credential offer is not shared just between user and Keycloak, but needs to be shared with multiple parties (administrator, which created offer. Eventually application, which triggered the REST. This is more a problem for pre-authorized code grant, but applies to authorization-code as well)

**Usability:** Once offer created by admin, it needs to be shared somehow with the user by some channel out-of-scope of Keycloak. Since Keycloak is OOTB authorization and identity server, it is generally preferable if most of the things are handled by Keycloak itself rather than a requirement to be "outsourced" to different parties, which would need to handle sharing of credential-offer by some other channels.

**Coarse-grained permission:** “Administrator” with realm role `credential-offer-create` can create offer for anyone. It is in fact admin permission, but not integrated into proper Keycloak admin REST API.

**Allows long expiration:** User can create lots of offers (entries in the action-tokens cache) with long expiration. Possible DoS/memory leak


### Value Proposition

Value is unclear right now as in Keycloak 26.8, we have other ways for creating credential offers, which is either:
 
- AIA (application-initiated action), which can be triggered by user himself (Keycloak account console uses this)
- admin console + admin REST API for the administrator creating offer for the user, which is sent to user's email

Those are consistent with other Keycloak functionality and leverages other Keycloak built-in blocks (account + admin console, admin permissions, AIA, sending email functionality etc)

At the same time, there are likely some valid use-cases when this feature is desired? 
**For anyone from the community:** Please add the comment to this issue with your use-case if the supported way of creating credential offers in 26.8 does not work for you and you would prefer this feature to be prioritized for the promotion to preview. Eventually add "thumbs-up" to the existing comment if your use-case is same/similar as some other mentioned comment.
   

### Goals

- Validate if the `OID4VC_VCI_REST_CREDENTIAL_OFFER` should be either supported or removed

### Non-Goals

- 

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: [OID4VCI] Revisit/support credential offer created by REST endpoint

### Description

When migrating from legacy V1 token exchange (external-to-internal) to the new V2 JWT Authorization Grant (urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer), identity provider mappers configured on the external IdP are ignored.  This is affecting some customers who are trying to migrate to v2. 

In V1 token exchange, Keycloak ran the Identity Provider's configured mappers on incoming external tokens. In V2 (JWT Authorization Grant), Keycloak ignores all mappers and only looks for an existing linked user. Because no mappers run, several critical customer use cases are broken:I

1. Customers cannot dynamically link incoming external identities to existing Keycloak user accounts at request time. If the link does not already exist, the request simply fails with "User not found".
2. Assigning roles or attributes (e.g., Hardcoded Role Mapper): Standard IdP mappers configured in the Admin Console (such as assigning default roles or mapping claims to user attributes based on the external IdP) do not execute.
3. Subject and alias transformation: In environments where the external token's subject identifier needs to be transformed or sanitized before matching the local account, there is no way to adapt the identity.

### Value Proposition

Enables customers with external identity federation workflows to migrate from deprecated V1 token exchange to the standards-based RFC 7523 JWT Authorization Grant without losing essential user provisioning, auto-linking, and role/attribute mapping capabilities.

### Goals

Support running Identity Provider mappers during the JWT Authorization Grant flow.
Allow dynamic matching/linking of external identities to existing Keycloak users.
Ensure configured IdP mappers (e.g., role, attribute, and claim mappers) apply when exchanging external JWT assertions.

### Non-Goals

Changing the deprecated V1 token exchange flow.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_
issues.title: Support Identity Provider Mappers in Token Exchange V2 and JWT Authorization Grant

### Description

Many identity provider support some concept of tenants. 

For example Google allows sending the `hd` param in the auth request, which will also be included in the returned tokens. Keycloak supports the `Hosted Domain` option for Google, but does not have a generic mechanism that can be used with other providers.

There's a [draft specification](https://openid.github.io/connect-enterprise-extensions/main.html#name-tenant) around this, but it's been draft for a while and even if it was made final it would take some time before all providers would support it.

It should be possible to configure a tenant when setting up any IdP that supports a tenant concept. In reality that means providing 3 configuration options:

* The tenant id
* An optional query parameter to send the tenant id when doing an auth request to the provider
* The claim name to verify in the tokens issued by the provider

Specific providers that we have like Google would set hard-code these so only the tenant id would have to be configurable.

When adding support for tenants we would need to make sure that all use-cases such as user federation, client federation, and authorization grants, verify the claim.

### Value Proposition

In many use-cases only a specific tenant should be permitted to authenticate with Keycloak, by limiting this to the required tenant it prevents other users/clients in the provider from authenticated with Keycloak, which increases security.

### Goals

* Support a configurable tenant concept for the generic OIDC provider
* Leverage the above in all specific providers that have a tenant concept where the parameter name and claim name is known, allowing only configuring the tenant id.

### Non-Goals

* Add generic support for verifying any claim; this will be limited to a single claim aka tenants use-case.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

_No response_

### Description

## Description

I would like to request an additional **"Groups in role"** tab in the Keycloak Admin Console, similar to the existing **"Users in role"** tab.

Currently, when selecting a realm role, administrators can see which users have that role. However, there is no equivalent overview showing which groups have been assigned that role.

While it is possible to inspect the role mappings of each individual group, there is no convenient way to view this relationship from the role's perspective.

## Motivation

In many Keycloak environments, roles are primarily assigned to groups rather than directly to individual users.

When managing permissions or troubleshooting role assignments, it is important to quickly identify which groups are associated with a specific role.

Currently, administrators need to navigate through individual groups and inspect their role mappings, which can be time-consuming, especially in realms with many groups.

## Proposed Solution

Add a **"Groups in role"** tab to the role details page in the Admin Console, alongside the existing "Users in role" tab.

The new tab should:

- Display all groups directly assigned to the selected role.
- Show the group name and full group path.
- Allow administrators to navigate directly to a group's details.
- Support pagination for environments with many groups.

Ideally, this should be supported for both realm roles and client roles.

## Technical Considerations

The required information is already available through the Keycloak Admin REST API:

For realm roles:
`GET /admin/realms/{realm}/roles/{role-name}/groups`

For client roles:
`GET /admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{client-uuid}/roles/{role-name}/groups`

Therefore, this feature could potentially be implemented primarily as an Admin Console enhancement using existing API endpoints.

### Value Proposition

This feature would provide a more consistent and intuitive administration experience, especially for organizations that primarily manage role assignments through groups.

It would simplify permission auditing, troubleshooting, and role management by allowing administrators to quickly identify which groups are associated with a specific role, without having to inspect each group individually.

### Goals

- Add a  **"Groups in role"** tab to the role details page in the Keycloak Admin Console, similar to the existing "Users in role" tab.
- Display all groups that are directly assigned to the selected role.
- Show the group name and full group path.
- Allow administrators to navigate directly to the corresponding group.
- Support both realm roles and client roles.
- Reuse the existing Keycloak Admin REST API endpoints.

### Non-Goals

- No changes to the existing role assignment or permission model.
- No modification of group-to-role mappings directly from the new tab.
- No changes to how users inherit roles through group membership.
- No introduction of new REST API endpoints, as the required functionality is already available through the existing Admin REST API.

### Discussion

- Should the new "Groups in role" tab follow the same UI patterns and behavior as the existing "Users in role" tab? 
- Should the initial implementation display only direct group-to-role assignments, with indirect assignments through composite roles considered separately? 
- Are there any technical or UX considerations that would favor a different approach?  Feedback and alternative implementation suggestions are welcome.

### Notes

This feature request primarily concerns the Keycloak Admin Console.

The existing Admin REST API already provides endpoints for retrieving groups associated with realm roles and client roles.

Therefore, the implementation may be possible without introducing new backend functionality or modifying the existing role assignment model.

The proposed tab should follow the existing Admin Console design conventions to ensure a consistent user experience.
issues.title: Add "Groups in role" tab to Realm Roles in Admin Console
